rationale: B wins because it treats the study as a liability gate, not just a shiny topline. Its "The company that sells the app paid for the study that says the app works" angle forces the founder to prove the story before pitching; A's "Calm-funded study finds an 18% anxiety drop — who checked the math?" gets the right door open but stops at a more generic methods checklist. B has its own overreach, but its proof questions would save a founder from walking into a science reporter's trap.
gaps_in_A: "Insurers just made Calm a default benefit for 25 million Americans" overstates the update: the facts say a covered no-cost benefit for insurer members, not a default benefit, and not explicitly Americans.

"Are health insurers using a meditation app instead of paying for real anxiety care?" frames substitution before evidence. The update says Calm was added as a covered benefit, not that therapy or psychiatric access was reduced.
"live, recurring skeptical thread in digital-mental-health coverage" gestures at a policy backdrop without supplied evidence. If that debate matters, verify the peg or keep it out of the angle.

The next step jumps to `find-journalists` after insurer names and journal citation, but the 18% claim also needs a fact-check/methodology gate before anyone pitches a science or health-policy reporter.
gaps_in_B: "at a moment when demand for care exceeds clinician supply" invents a public-health backdrop. The set later admits no clinician-supply figure was supplied, so it knows better.
"on the plan's dime" implies the insurers are paying. The update explicitly says revenue terms were not disclosed.
"routing around app-store retail into employer and payer channels" adds an employer channel and a DTC-saturation theory not in the facts. Make it a question or cut it.
"category-creation" is bigger than the evidence. One Calm deal plus one company-funded study is not a category unless comparable payer coverage exists.
